title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We present the exact McNemar result as the preregistered confirmatory outcome, report the bootstrap CI as a preregistered descriptive summary, explicitly label a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) as exploratory/post‑hoc, and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, high baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations can reduce manual workload but raises safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that affect code and configuration generation, motivating architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1], [2].

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates purely downstream validator/repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Our precise research question is: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics), to what degree can a downstream deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes compared with reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design intentionally isolates downstream interventions (validation and at‑most‑one repair) so any paired difference is attributable to those downstream mechanisms rather than to first‑pass generation differences such as prompt engineering, constrained decoding, or sampling variance.

Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment (Npairs = 1000) with deterministic task selection from a synthetic stress corpus and archived validator traces; (2) full execution accounting and artifact grounding documenting provider calls, shared_initial semantics, and repair occurrences; (3) a transparent preregistered confirmatory inferential result (exact two‑sided McNemar) together with preregistered descriptive summaries and an explicit distinction between confirmatory and exploratory analyses.
sections.related_work:
Empirical and survey work documents hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures for LLMs applied to code and configuration tasks [2], [3]. Schema‑constrained decoding and intent‑to‑execution frameworks reduce syntactic and executability errors in structured domains, though most demonstrations outside NetOps use domain‑specific validators [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers emphasize verifier‑assisted repair, guarded architectures, and governance/proof‑carrying proposals that argue operational reliability depends on validator coverage and enforcement protocols rather than on any single model alone [4], [5], [6].

Our study complements these works by preregistering a paired comparison whose estimand isolates the incremental effect of deterministic downstream validation and a single limited repair call when the initial candidate is held constant across conditions; this avoids conflation with first‑pass generation interventions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was frozen before any hosted‑model invocation (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest = ab4c6436c6ece56bf47da7730d50485a17cdb9bb86a90a4231042303d3b489ec). Key prespecifications: confirmatory paired binary design; task_count = 1000 deterministic tasks drawn from challenging_workflow_stress_v1; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair deterministically reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary prespecified summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) and sensitivity analyses for failure treatments.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and interpretive consequences. Under shared_initial_candidate both baseline and guarded episodes begin from the same sampled initial candidate; the guarded pipeline can reject that candidate via deterministic validation and may invoke at most one permitted repair call. Therefore, paired outcome differences can only arise from deterministic validation decisions and permitted repair(s). This design does not measure effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generations, alternative prompts, or constrained decoding arms that were not executed.

Model/runtime configuration and temperature caveat. The declared provider/model in execution/model_configuration.json is gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator v5.0), a digital‑twin emulator enforcing workflow policies, required command presence and order, protected‑field noninterference, and emitting a deterministic safe‑deploy verdict.

Task corpus and selection. Tasks were deterministically selected using the preregistered ordinal rule producing exactly 1000 unique tasks; each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty labels (very_hard, extreme). Difficulty composition in the executed corpus: extreme = 200 tasks (20.0%), very_hard = 800 tasks (80.0%).

Execution accounting, retries, and missingness. Retries were limited per preregistration (maximum_attempts_per_call = 1). The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 2000, failed_episode_count = 0, hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5}. The preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' missingness treatment was applied; sensitivity analyses treating failures as unsafe were preregistered but not required because failed episodes = 0.

Statistical analysis. The prespecified confirmatory test is the exact two‑sided McNemar on the 2×2 paired contingency table. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was prespecified as a descriptive secondary summary. No one‑sided McNemar was prespecified; any such one‑sided result reported below is explicitly exploratory/post‑hoc.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run completed all planned episodes (planned = 2000; completed = 2000; complete_pairs = 1000). Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005 with stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5} and no failed model calls. All deterministic consistency checks passed and contamination checks found no prompt‑leakage flags.

Paired outcomes and preregistered inferential test. The 2×2 paired contingency table is n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The prespecified primary confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625, which does not meet the prespecified two‑sided α = 0.05 threshold; therefore the preregistered H1 is not supported by the confirmatory analysis.

Secondary descriptive summaries and repair diagnostics. The prespecified paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred; representative archived episode artifacts show validators rejecting initial candidates for required_sequence or protected_interface violations and accepting repaired candidates after a single permitted repair call. Total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). The five discordant pair identifiers and brief reason codes are archived (examples include pair-000101, pair-000253, pair-000541, pair-001117, pair-001525; each baseline episode scored INVALIDATION_FAILED while the guarded episode achieved VALID_CONFIGURATION after one repair).
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory hierarchy and interpretation. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar is the primary confirmatory analysis and did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was a prespecified descriptive summary and can exclude zero in regimes with very sparse discordant counts because percentile bootstrap bounds are sensitive to the discrete distribution of n10/n01 when discordances are rare; this descriptive outcome does not overturn the preregistered confirmatory null. Any one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) reported here is explicitly exploratory/post‑hoc because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Mechanistic and external validity notes. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics only downstream validation and permitted repairs can create paired differences; observed repairs (5 total) demonstrate that validator‑triggered repair can correct some ordering/sequence violations in this synthetic corpus. However, the very high baseline validity (99.5%) diverged from the preregistered power assumption (baseline ≈ 0.60), substantially reducing sensitivity to detect small absolute gains using the planned paired test. External validity is limited by single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task corpus, and the validator rule set; follow‑ups should vary generation semantics, repair budgets, validator coverage, and model families with preregistered power calculations matched to plausible baseline failure rates.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus with shared_initial_candidate semantics, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the prespecified exact two‑sided McNemar confirmatory test did not reach significance at α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked. These artifact‑grounded results indicate that verifier‑guided repair can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflow settings, but measurable marginal gains depend strongly on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and repair budget. All preregistration, execution, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run to support reproducibility and targeted preregistered follow‑ups that broaden model diversity, validator coverage, and repair budgets.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
